body_markdown:
I try to be a neutral car lover most of the time. However, I still cannot fathom Lincoln, one of my favorite luxury makes, killing off all sedans after the 2020 model year. One would think that they at least would have kept either the MKZ or the Continental in production, to keep people who do not want SUVs (like your author) in the fold.


Lincoln


Sadly, they did not, and your author now drives a Cadillac XTS Luxury. Which I love. And the fine folks at McLaughlin Cadillac take excellent care of it. But if Lincoln had still offered a sedan, I might yet have one. And if they decide to reintroduce one, perhaps they could add at least a bit of the style and swagger of today’s featured ’72 Connie sedan—in all its glorious chrome, hidden headlights, and brutal, squared-off looks.


Jayson Coombes


35,561 sedans were built, with a 4958-lb curb weight and $7302 MSRP. The Continental coupe was $7068; the personal luxury Continental Mark IV, $8640. In addition to White, other hues included Pastel Lime, Dark Brown, Dark Blue Metallic, Dark Green Metallic, Light Ginger Moondust, Red Moondust, Maroon, and Light Yellow Gold. Under the hood was a 460-cubic-inch V-8 with a four-barrel carburetor. Michelin tires were standard.


Jayson Coombes


The classic 1961-69 Continentals are widely favored and collected these days—especially the ’61-67 convertibles, but by the end of the Sixties they were a little long in the tooth. A new design was decided upon, and in Autumn of 1969 the first ’70 Continentals appeared in showrooms.


Jayson Coombes


Perhaps the biggest change was the loss of those center-opening doors. As I have read in the past, the change was made in an attempt to lure in customers of “The other luxury car make,” as Lincoln tactfully referred to their arch-rival, Cadillac.


Jayson Coombes


While the 1970-71 lost the chrome trim atop the fender blades, doors, and rear quarter panels as had been seen on the classic 1961-69 models, starting in 1972, along with some other minor refinements, it returned.


Jayson Coombes


A checkerboard grille replaced the formal Cord-inspired horizontal bar unit, and the pronounced Coke-bottle rear fenders were squared off a bit, with the rear door handles moved lower, in line with the front handles.


Jayson Coombes


Today’s example was spied by my friend Jayson Coombes at the LCOC Eastern Meet in Knoxville, Tennessee, back in 2023. It looked really imposing in White (as Lincoln called it; no snazzy names like Cotillion White, over at Cadillac) with a “slick top” (no vinyl roof) and matching, sumptuous white leather with a black instrument panel and carpeting.


Jayson Coombes


The Continental sedans are a bit overshadowed by collectors these days, when compared to the Mark IIIs and Mark IVs when it comes to 1970s Lincolns, but I will always love them!
